sentence: I have logged thirty-two unsolicited calls from your company in the last month. Thirty-two. I have screenshots of all of them. I have the carrier records. I have the FCC complaint number assigned to my case. The next call you make to this number will be the basis for legal action, and I am genuinely excited about it. Bring it. I am ready. I have been waiting for someone to actually answer for this nightmare.

Suspending the wrong player for a hit committed by his teammate, then refusing to overturn the suspension when the video evidence is overwhelming, is the kind of corruption-adjacent incompetence that should end careers. The league office is staffed by people who have apparently never watched a game. Their decisions land like physics problems solved by someone who has never met gravity. Embarrassing on a global scale.

The streaming app I have been paying for since 2018 just decided that my account needs to verify a new device every time I switch from the TV to my phone, then demands a code from an email that arrives twenty minutes late, then logs me out completely if I do not enter it within sixty seconds. They want me to cancel. They are engineering me into canceling. And the cynical part is that they will then offer me a sixty percent discount to come back, which I will refuse, on principle, until I forget I was ever angry.

I have requested removal from this mailing list six times. Six. Each time the company assures me that it can take up to ninety days for the change to take effect. Ninety days has elapsed five times. The mail keeps coming. The mail will always keep coming. The opt-out is a fiction, a soothing lie that the company tells customers so they feel like they have done something. They have done nothing. I have done nothing. The mail wins.

I have eaten in hospital cafeterias, prison waiting rooms, and a gas station in rural Idaho, and not one of those places served food as offensively bad as what came out of that kitchen. The pad thai was wet cardboard. The spring rolls were greased rubber. The dipping sauce was an act of aggression. Every single dish tasted like it was prepared by someone who hates eating and resents the customers for doing it.

The cookie consent banner is so aggressive that it covers the entire page and refuses to dismiss until I have manually deselected sixty-seven different vendor categories. The reject all button is buried two clicks deep, behind a manage settings screen, behind a confirmation, behind a please reconsider dialog. The accept all button is enormous, brightly colored, and clearly meant to be the path of least resistance. The whole UX is engineered to break me.

I am not the only one this happened to. There are seventeen of us in a group chat at this point, all reporting the same experience, all with the same screenshots of the same boilerplate apology email that promises a refund that never arrives. This is not a series of unfortunate incidents. This is a pattern. This is a business model. And I am going to make sure every potential customer searches the company name and finds this post sitting at the top of the results.

Telling me my Halloween decorations are excessive is the kind of bored petulance that gives every HOA in America a bad name. They are seasonal. They are temporary. They are loved by every child on this street. The fact that the HOA president has decided his personal taste is the law of the land tells me he has too much power and not enough hobbies. The decorations are staying. The fines are going to small claims. Bring it on.

The outage map says my entire neighborhood is offline and your chat agent just told me my connection is healthy. It is not healthy. It is dead. I am typing this on my phone using cellular data because the internet I pay you to provide has gone the way of the dodo for the third time today. Stop reading your script and look out a window.

I came back to my car to find a note that said I could have parked closer to the line. The note was passive-aggressive. The note was unsigned. The note was scrawled on the back of a receipt. I was inside the lines. I checked. Whoever wrote that note is the kind of person who has the time and energy to inspect other people's parking jobs, and the lack of self-awareness to think this was a reasonable use of their afternoon. Touch grass.

The garage is full. The sign at the entrance says it is full. The attendant waves me through anyway, takes my money, and then watches me drive up six levels finding no spaces. When I come back down to complain, he tells me to try the lot across the street, no refund. The grift is breathtaking. The casual dishonesty is the most upsetting part. He charged me money he knew I could not use, and he did not even pretend it was a mistake.

Your sources are a blog post from 2011, a video by some guy in his basement, and a tweet from an account with seventeen followers. That is not research. That is the digital equivalent of asking the loudest guy at the bar to settle an argument. Come back when you have something approaching legitimate evidence, or do not come back at all. The forum will be just fine without your contributions.

Block me. Just block me. I would block you if I had not already decided that watching you embarrass yourself in real time was a strange form of public service. Every single post of yours reads like a parody account of a worse version of yourself. The mods should ban you not for being a troll but for lowering the average IQ of the entire subforum every time you post.

The investment seminar disguised as a free financial planning workshop is a scam. The high-pressure sales pitch at the end of the free dinner is the scam. The hidden fees in the contract you signed before reading carefully are the scam. The whole industry of fleecing retirees out of their nest eggs is built on a thousand small deceptions, each one technically legal, all of them adding up to ruin. Regulators, where are you?

The car company is now charging a monthly fee to use the heated seats that are already physically installed in the vehicle I paid sixty thousand dollars for. The hardware is in the car. The wires are connected. The chip is sitting there doing nothing. They have decided that the laws of property no longer apply and that I must rent functions of the metal box I supposedly own. This is theft with a chrome finish.

Every mortgage refinance company in a hundred-mile radius now has my address. They have all sent me identical letters this month. They have all printed my name in a slightly off shade of black that looks fraudulent on purpose. They all reference my current loan in a way designed to alarm me. None of them have ever spoken to me. None of them know my financial situation. They are spamming the mailbox of every homeowner in the zip code and counting on a fraction of one percent biting.

Every single time I open this app it forces me to update. I update. It works for a day. It demands another update. I update. It crashes on launch. I update again. It works for two hours. It demands a third update. The version number is climbing into the absurd. I am running version 17.4.92.delta-3 of a calculator app. A calculator. The thing has one job. It has had thirty updates this year.

The covered procedure that turned out not to be covered, after the surgery, after the recovery, after I had already paid the out-of-pocket portion, is the kind of post-hoc denial that has destroyed family finances across this country. The insurance company knew it was excluded the whole time. They processed the pre-approval. They received the bill. And then they sent a denial six months later, when the bill was already mine. Pure malice in business form.

Someone has stacked all five thousand pounds of plates on a single leg press and left them there. They are not coming back. The plates have been abandoned for fifteen minutes. No one wants to unrack them because no one came to the gym to spend twenty minutes removing one man's vanity weight. The gym has become a graveyard of inconsiderate setups and the rest of us are tip-toeing around the headstones.

The internet has decided that this minor celebrity scandal is the most important thing happening on the planet, and millions of otherwise intelligent adults are spending hours of their lives arguing about it with strangers. There are real things happening. There are real problems. The fact that we have collectively chosen to use our limited attention on this petty nonsense is a civilizational embarrassment.

The card reader is asking me if I want to round up to support a charity. It is asking me if I want to add a tip. It is asking me to enter a phone number. It is asking me to enter an email. It is asking me if I would like to apply for a store credit card. I want to pay. I want to leave. I want to go home. Every prompt is another second I lose to the corporation, and every customer behind me is silently rooting for me to skip them all without insulting the cashier.

I do not care what your contractor told you about property lines. I care what the survey says, and the survey is in my filing cabinet, and the survey says your new fence is twenty inches inside my yard. Move it back or I will move it back, and you can explain to the next set of contractors why they need to redo work that was illegal to begin with. The audacity of building on someone else's land and expecting them to just accept it.

The store has just opened a new register. Customers from the back of the line are sprinting to it while those of us who have been waiting patiently are stuck where we are because moving means losing our place. The cashier at the new register is laughing. The opportunists are laughing. The fairness of the universe has died on aisle nine and no one is coming to mourn it.

The search bar is offering me suggestions that have nothing to do with what I am typing. I am typing the name of a town. The suggestions include unrelated products, celebrity gossip, and a question someone else apparently asked last week. The autocomplete is not finishing my thought. The autocomplete is interrupting my thought with someone else's thought. The whole interface is a noisy chaperone preventing me from arriving at the result I came for.

The rental car was advertised at sixty dollars a day. The final bill is two hundred and forty dollars a day after the airport facility charge, the customer facility fee, the vehicle license recovery fee, the energy recovery fee, the concession recovery fee, the additional driver fee, and three different insurance products that were aggressively up-sold by the counter agent who would not let me finalize the transaction without acknowledging each one. The car is the same car. The destination is the same place. The price is a fiction wrapped in disclaimers.

Stop trying to coach strangers. I did not ask for tips on my deadlift form. The fact that you have decided you are the gym's volunteer instructor is the kind of patronizing nonsense that makes women avoid this place. I have been lifting longer than you have been alive. I know what I am doing. Mind your own workout. The exit is over there if you cannot help yourself.

I had a live presentation to seventy clients this morning. Forty seconds in, the connection died. By the time I rejoined on my phone hotspot, half the room had logged off and the other half was assuming I had abandoned ship. I lost a contract over this. A real one. With real money attached. And your billing department had the audacity to charge me full rate for the month during which your service worked for approximately thirty-eight percent of the hours I needed it.

The free trial was three days long and required a credit card and full address upfront. The renewal charge hit at midnight on day three, before I had a chance to evaluate the product at all. The product is mediocre. The pricing model is predatory. The refund request was denied because by accessing the service I had, according to the terms, used it. Used it for what. Three days of orientation videos and a tutorial that crashed twice.

Stop hogging three pieces of equipment for your superset routine. The gym is full. There are people waiting. Your circuit training is not more important than my ability to use the squat rack. Get a home gym if you cannot share equipment with strangers. The whole point of paying a monthly membership is that we collectively share these machines, and you are weaponizing your workout to monopolize them. Move along.

He told me to use a different font in the report. He told me which font. He told me which font size. He told me which color the headers should be. He told me the spacing between paragraphs. He told me to use bullet points instead of numbered lists, then ten minutes later told me to use numbered lists instead of bullet points. The content of the report is irrelevant to him. The formatting is the work. I am being paid to be his typesetter.

I am writing to inform you that I will never, ever, under any circumstance, fly your airline again, and I will be telling everyone I know to avoid you at all costs. You lost my luggage for nine days. Nine days. With my medication in it. The representative I finally reached suggested I just go buy new toiletries, as if my prescription antidepressants were a tube of toothpaste. Disgraceful.

Two tables that arrived twenty minutes after us have ordered, eaten, and paid while we sit here still staring at our menus like archaeological specimens. The server, who I now suspect is a hologram, drifts past every few minutes promising to be right with us. He has never been right with us. He will never be right with us. We are ghosts in this restaurant and it is time to haunt somewhere else.

The insurance solicitation arrived in a window envelope designed to look exactly like a government document. The return address contains a string of letters meant to evoke an official agency. The contents are entirely commercial. The targeting is grandparents and elderly people who are still trained to take mail seriously. The whole industry of dressing up sales pitches as official correspondence should be illegal and is not, because the people who would make it illegal are also benefiting from the practice in ways no one will admit.

Every single treadmill is taken and there is a line of people pretending not to be a line. Each user has set their machine for sixty minutes. The gym has a thirty minute limit posted on signs every twenty feet, which everyone is studiously ignoring. The staff at the front desk are watching this happen and doing nothing. The rule is a fiction. The line is a fiction. The polite veneer of the gym is fraying and I am ready to start enforcing the rules personally.

I asked the smart assistant to set a timer and it ordered me a pound of timer-related products from a third-party retailer. The order has shipped. I cannot cancel because the assistant placed the order on a payment method I do not recognize, which is apparently linked to my account in a way I never approved. The mystery vendor will appear at my doorstep tomorrow with a box of items I never requested, and the assistant remains cheerful about all of this.

The CEO's statement says he is deeply sorry for the harm caused, that the company takes full responsibility, and that they are committed to doing better. He did not write this. A team of lawyers and a public relations consultant wrote this. They wrote it the day before the scandal broke because they knew the scandal was coming and they had time to prepare a script. The apology is theater. The harm continues. Nothing changes.

The price check has been requested. The price check has been waiting on a price check for nine minutes. The price check person is on another aisle. The price check person is currently checking another price. The line has not moved. The customer whose item required the price check is now apologetic in a way that suggests they expect the rest of us to absolve them. We do not. We hold them personally responsible for our suffering.

The trailer promised a thriller. The film delivered a confused, meandering domestic drama with three explosions inserted at random intervals to remind us we were supposed to be on the edge of our seats. Bait and switch is fine in commerce. In cinema it is a crime against the audience. I want a refund and an apology from every studio executive who signed off on this marketing fraud.

I just spent forty-five minutes troubleshooting with your bot only to have it conclude that my service is operating within normal parameters. Normal parameters now apparently includes complete absence of signal for eight hours at a stretch. If that is normal you have set the bar in a trench beneath the sea floor and I am tired of paying premium prices for subterranean service.

An accident on the other side of the median has somehow brought my side of the freeway to a complete standstill. Why? What are you looking at? You cannot help. You will never help. You are just slowing down to gawk like an animal at a corpse, and dragging the productivity of an entire region down with you. Drive past. Drive past. Mind your own business and drive past.

I have been at the DMV for four hours. The line has moved exactly twelve people. There are nine windows. Two are open. The other seven employees are visibly present, drinking coffee, looking at their phones, having quiet conversations behind partial barriers. The number system has skipped me twice. The kiosk gave me the wrong category of ticket. The supervisor is on break. I have aged in this room. I will leave a different person than I entered.

Stop honking at me at red lights, you absolute psychopath. I am stopped because the light is red. The law requires me to stop at red lights. You sitting behind me leaning on your horn does not change the color of the light, it only confirms that you are a small, angry person with no understanding of how traffic signals work. Have some patience. Read a book. Develop an inner life. Just stop honking.

The banana taped to the wall sold for one hundred and twenty thousand dollars. The banana. Taped. To the wall. Whoever bought it deserves to lose every cent of it, and whoever sold it should be barred from the art world for a generation. We have all collectively agreed to participate in an emperor's new clothes situation that has gone so far past parody it has come around to genuine sadness. Real artists are starving while this nonsense gets headlines.

Hidden fees. Every bill is a treasure hunt for hidden fees. The broadcast fee. The regional sports fee. The franchise fee. The line maintenance fee. The fees somehow add up to more than the advertised rate. The advertised rate is a lie, dressed up to look like a deal, used to capture customers who do not have the time to audit a monthly bill for inventions of corporate accounting. I have the time now. And I am itemizing every fraudulent charge.

The retention department is full of people whose entire job is to make you feel like cancelling is a crime against the company. I am not your friend. I do not owe you loyalty. I want to leave because your service is bad and your prices are worse. End the call. Do not transfer me. Do not put me on hold while you check with a manager. Do not offer me a temporary discount that expires in ninety days. Just cancel.

The technician was scheduled for an eight to noon window. He showed up at four-thirty. Four-thirty. I took the entire day off work to wait for him. He spent fifteen minutes in my house, replaced a single cable, and left without testing whether the issue was resolved. It was not resolved. I had to call again, and the next available appointment is eleven days away. This is what monopoly looks like when no one is checking on it.

Whoever designed this update should be banned from touching software for the rest of their career. The menus that worked perfectly for ten years have been buried under three layers of cryptic icons, the keyboard shortcuts have all been changed for no reason, and a chatbot now interrupts me every thirty seconds to ask if I need help. I do need help. I need help from the previous version, which you destroyed for absolutely no reason except boredom.

Two hours of my life that I will never get back, set fire to by a director who clearly believes that loud noises and shaky cameras are substitutes for an actual story. The plot makes no sense. The characters are interchangeable. The dialogue sounds like it was generated by a malfunctioning chatbot with a thesaurus problem. Whoever greenlit this gibberish should be reassigned to mopping floors at the theater showing it, where they would at least be doing something useful.

The man at the cable machine has wrapped a towel around the handle, draped his water bottle on the seat, plugged in his phone, and walked off to use the bathroom for the past ten minutes. The towel claim has been recognized in gym culture as a sacred territorial marker. I do not recognize this culture. I am moving the towel. I am claiming the machine. He can fight me when he returns from his leisurely toilet visit.

I have explained the same situation to four different representatives in the last week, and not one of them has the authority to actually do anything about it. They can apologize. They can sympathize. They cannot fix. The entire customer service apparatus exists to absorb anger and produce nothing in return. It is a containment field. It is a moral failure dressed up as a department.

The close button is intentionally three pixels wide. The X is drawn in light gray on a white background. The hover area is a millimeter off from the visible target. When I click in the actual close zone, the ad opens in a new tab anyway because the entire area is a hyperlink masquerading as a close button. This is not a design flaw. This is a strategy. They have hired engineers to do this on purpose.

Two hours waiting for a steak that arrived cold, gray, and apparently apologizing for its own existence. The manager had the gall to suggest I order something else and pay for both, like I was the one who'd done something wrong. I have never been so insulted by a piece of meat in my life. The whole place reeked of old grease and managerial incompetence. Burn it down and start over.

Three executives have spent the last twenty minutes reading their slides aloud to a room full of literate adults. I can read. Everyone in this room can read. The slides are projected on the wall. They are also distributed in the deck attached to the calendar invite. They have been read three times. Reading them again will not change them. Reading them again will not summon insight. Reading them again is a torture I did not consent to.

I have not asked for your opinion. I have not asked for your guidance. I have not asked for your wisdom. I have not asked for your story about how you went through something similar twenty years ago and learned the following lesson. I am venting. The appropriate response to venting is a brief expression of sympathy, not a lecture. The fact that I have to explain this to a grown adult is itself a small tragedy.

The squat rack has been occupied for fifty minutes by a man doing curls. Curls. With a barbell that he then unloads and walks away from, leaving the rack tied up while he goes to the water fountain. The rack is for squats. The squats are why the rack exists. There are nine other places in the gym he could be curling. He has chosen the rack because it has a place to lean. I am ready to start a one-man movement to claim the rack by force.

The benefits office requires an in-person interview. The next available in-person interview is in seventeen weeks. The benefits would have expired four months ago by that date. The office acknowledges this. The office cannot do anything about it. The office suggests reapplying after the lapse, which restarts the clock, and which guarantees I will lose access to the benefits I rely on. This is not bureaucracy. This is institutional cruelty.

I have been paying premiums for sixteen years. Sixteen years. The one time I needed to file a claim, the insurance company opened an investigation into my medical history, demanded documentation from doctors I saw two decades ago, and ultimately denied the claim on a technicality that did not exist when I bought the policy. They changed the terms. They never told me. The whole industry is built on this exact predatory pattern, and the regulators look the other way.

Why are the crew of the canceled flight all sitting at the bar across from my gate while we are being told there is no available crew to operate a replacement? They are right there. I can see them. I can hear them laughing. Either your operations team does not communicate with your scheduling team, or they have decided that the truth is too inconvenient to tell paying customers. Either way, the situation is unacceptable. Fix your business.

Filming your workout on three different cameras simultaneously while taking up the entire mirror section is a level of self-absorption that I cannot put up with anymore. The mirror is not yours. The lighting is not yours. The floor is not your personal studio. The other members of this gym did not consent to being extras in your YouTube channel. Pack it up, find a corner, or join one of those influencer-only facilities you keep posting about.

The footnotes outnumber the actual narrative. The acknowledgments section is six pages long and mostly thanks the author's editor for putting up with him, which is the closest thing to honesty the entire book contains. The novel itself is a slog. The structure is incoherent. The prose alternates between purple and beige with no warning. I finished it because I had committed to reviewing it. I would not recommend that anyone else make the same mistake.

I watched our server take an order to a four-top, return to the kitchen, exchange a long laugh with the line cook, refill the manager's coffee, restock the bread baskets at the front, take a phone call, and then drift over to a different table entirely while ours sat untouched. We were here first. We have been here longest. We are leaving last. I will not be back, and I will be telling everyone I know exactly why.

I was told to come back tomorrow. Tomorrow I was told to come back next week. Next week I was told that the policy had changed and the form I had spent a month preparing was no longer valid. Months of work erased by a memo no one bothered to publish. Hours of my life consumed by an institution that treats its own citizens like an inconvenience. I want my time back. I want it all back.

There are now ads inside the ads. The pre-roll has a banner. The pop-up has a sidebar. The autoplay video has overlay text promoting a second product. The internet is no longer a place. It is a billboard surrounded by other billboards surrounded by billboards billing me for the privilege of looking at them. I miss the era when ads were on the page next to the content rather than dressed up as content and shoved into my face.

The tone of your last message was so condescending that I had to read it three times to confirm I was not imagining it. I am not your intern. I am not your protege. I have been doing this longer than you have been at the company, and I do not need a junior analyst lecturing me about best practices in an industry he has been in for eight months. Step back. Way back.

Three weeks after the disaster, they issued an apology and a fifteen-dollar gift card. Fifteen dollars. To affected customers whose accounts were drained, whose data was leaked, and whose lives were upended by an executive decision to skip a security audit because it was inconvenient. The gift card is for use only at their own store. You cannot even use it elsewhere. The audacity is enough to make you want to drive to corporate headquarters and stand on the lawn shouting.

Three hundred and twelve dollars a month. Three hundred and twelve. For a service that drops out the moment a cloud passes overhead and a router that requires a restart every forty-eight hours just to maintain basic function. The technician they sent over to fix it spent forty minutes blaming my electrical wiring and then left without resolving anything. I am being robbed in slow motion by a company with no competitor in my zip code, and there is nothing I can do about it.

Why does it require six weeks to process a request that consists of a single yes-or-no decision based on information already in your possession? The same agencies that can mail me a tax bill within forty-eight hours of a missed deadline somehow cannot return a phone call about an open case within six months. The asymmetry is by design. The system works exactly as intended, and the intention is to wear citizens down.

The fact that we let supplement companies advertise miracle cures with no regulatory oversight is one of the great failures of modern consumer protection. The FDA has its hands tied. The companies are getting rich. The customers are getting hurt. Every other commercial break on daytime television is a man with a fake doctor title selling pills that have never been tested. We are sleepwalking through a slow-motion scandal.

Your kids have been throwing balls into my yard every single afternoon for the last two weeks and then climbing my fence to retrieve them. Not asking. Climbing. They have broken three plants and trampled my vegetables. Either teach them some manners or buy them a backyard of their own, because mine is no longer available as a community sports field. I have stopped tossing the balls back. I am keeping them now.

The board members of this HOA have somehow decided that a power trip about lawn length is a substitute for actual community building. We are paying hundreds of dollars a month for a clubhouse no one uses, a pool that closes early, and a roving inspector with a clipboard. Where is the money going? Into envelopes. Into perks for the board. Into legal fees defending the lawsuits the board itself has provoked. We need a recall election yesterday.

The HOA spent forty-seven thousand dollars on a new entrance sign that looks exactly like the old one. The board approved it unanimously, with no resident input, after rejecting three less-expensive proposals because they did not feel premium enough. We are paying for this with our dues. Our dues, which somehow keep going up while the visible services keep going down. There is corruption in this building and the auditors should be investigating.

I have been a loyalty member for fifteen years. Fifteen years of putting up with your shrinking seats, your vanishing services, your rising fees. And when I needed a single flight change due to a family emergency, you charged me four hundred dollars and gave me a middle seat. That is not a relationship. That is a hostage situation. I am taking my business elsewhere, and I hope every other long-term customer does the same.

The roofing company has sent me a flyer every week for the last fourteen months. I do not need a new roof. I do not own a house that needs a new roof. I rent. The roof is the landlord's problem. The roofing company does not care. The roofing company is operating on a strategy of attrition, hoping that eventually my roof will need replacing and I will be too worn down to choose a different company. They have miscalculated. I will choose any other company purely out of spite.

What a colossal waste of a hundred-fifty-million-dollar budget. The CGI looked like a video game from 2003. The sets were obviously plastic. The villain monologue went on for so long I lost track of why we were supposed to care. There are independent films made on a shoestring that look better, sound better, and mean more than this bloated, joyless, soulless piece of corporate sludge. Studios should be ashamed.

The mail-in renewal arrived three months after I sent it back, with a note that the renewal had been processed but the new card was not enclosed and would arrive in a separate envelope, which has not arrived. The note is the only proof that the renewal happened. The system shows nothing. The phone agents cannot find the record. I am being told to wait six to eight more weeks, which would put me past the expiration date of the very document I renewed.

The neighbor has stopped by, again, to suggest improvements to my landscaping. He has thoughts on the tree placement. He has thoughts on the mulch choice. He has thoughts on the bird feeder. He has thoughts on the color of the front door. His own yard is a chaos of unmown grass and abandoned lawn furniture. The brazen disconnect between his expertise and his execution is breathtaking. I have stopped opening the door when I see him approaching.

The form will not accept my address because the apartment number field is required, even though I do not live in an apartment. I have entered N/A. I have entered None. I have entered zero. I have entered the word house. The form rejects all of them. The dropdown for apartment number contains only floors of buildings the form thinks I might live in. I am not in any of those buildings. The form does not believe me.

The airline ticket included a fee to select a seat. A fee to bring a carry-on. A fee to print the boarding pass at the gate. A fee to check in earlier than two hours before the flight. A fee for early boarding. A fee for water on board. The base fare is now a notional figure that has no relationship to the price I actually pay. The base fare is a recruiting poster. The actual ticket is whatever they decide to extract from you over the course of the booking process.

Three packages were stacked on top of each other in front of the door, blocking the door from opening. I had to climb out the side window to retrieve them. The driver knew the door opened outward. He had been here before. He chose this configuration as a kind of malicious art installation. I am tempted to leave a thank-you note that he will find genuinely confusing.

The mobile experience is worse. There is no escape on mobile. The X button on the ad is somewhere off the bottom of the visible screen. Scrolling to find it triggers another ad. Tapping on the page accidentally opens the ad. Tapping precisely on the small piece of text that is the actual article also opens the ad. The mobile site has been engineered as a trap. There is no reading. There is only ad consumption with side garnish of journalism.

The romance scammer that strung my coworker along for two years took her entire retirement savings before she figured out what was happening. He sent her photographs of someone he was not, told her stories about a future they would never have, and slowly drained her finances under the pretext of medical emergencies. That man is somewhere right now, doing the same thing to someone else. I would like to know his name.

The supermarket flyer arrived crumpled, soaking wet, half illegible, and advertising prices that expired three days ago. The chain has spent money to manufacture, print, distribute, and deliver this object, all of which I will spend three seconds removing from my mailbox and depositing into the bin. The transaction has cost them several cents and me an entire moment of my limited life on this planet. Multiply this by every household in the country.

I missed my own father's funeral because of this airline's incompetence. There is no apology adequate. There is no voucher that fixes this. There is no future flight I will ever take with this carrier again. The CEO needs to look me in the eye and explain why a flight that left the previous afternoon was canceled while I was already at the airport. He will not, of course. He never does. He is paid millions to dodge this exact conversation.

The new parking app requires a separate account for each city, charges a transaction fee on top of the meter rate, and crashes every other time you open it. The previous quarters-in-the-meter system was instantaneous, universal, and reliable. We replaced it with something worse, more expensive, and slower, because someone in a startup convinced the city council it was innovation. It is not innovation. It is a tax disguised as technology.

They apologized for the inconvenience. The inconvenience. An entire municipal water supply contaminated for nine months and they called it an inconvenience. People got sick. Pets died. Property values cratered. They have framed a public health catastrophe in the language of a delayed shipment. If I never hear the phrase apologize for any inconvenience again it will be too soon, and I will personally chase down anyone who uses it in this context.

Your leaf blower starts at seven in the morning on a Saturday and runs for ninety minutes. Ninety. Minutes. There are not that many leaves on the planet. There certainly are not that many on your yard. You are not removing leaves anymore, you are conducting an aggressive sonic ritual against the entire block. Some of us work nights. Some of us have children. Some of us are this close to losing it. Buy a rake.

The voice menu just told me to say my reason for calling in plain English and then immediately misunderstood the word billing as building three separate times before transferring me to dental services. I do not have dental insurance with you. I do not have any insurance with you. I want to cancel the thing I never signed up for and your robot is gaslighting me into believing I have teeth problems. Put a human on the line or I am driving to your headquarters.

I left detailed instructions on the order page. I left a sign on the door. I texted the driver through the app. The package was nonetheless left in the rain in the worst possible spot, on a part of the porch with no overhang, six feet from the dry covered porch space clearly indicated by the sign and instructions. The contents were ruined. The driver claims he did not see the instructions. He did not look. He did not care. He did not want to.

I did not consent to the cloud. I did not ask for the cloud. The cloud is a marketing word for storing my files on a stranger's hard drive and charging me to access them. And now the app refuses to work offline, refuses to save locally by default, refuses to acknowledge that internet outages exist. When the wifi went down yesterday, I lost three hours of work that any normal program would have written safely to disk. Disgraceful design.

The application for a permit has been in processing for eleven months. Eleven months. The original estimate was four to six weeks. Every call to check on it produces the same answer, that it is still in processing and there is no further information available. There is a person somewhere who could tell me where my application is. That person is unreachable. There is no email address. There is no extension. There is no recourse. I am simply waiting and being told to keep waiting.

Boarding zones are a fiction you invented to make economy passengers feel inferior. By the time my zone seven is called, every overhead bin is full, every flight attendant is exhausted, and every chance of a peaceful flight has evaporated. The whole boarding process is a humiliation ritual designed to upsell premium seats. I see what you are doing. Everyone sees what you are doing. And we are all very tired of it.

The wellness industry has convinced an entire generation of otherwise rational adults that they need to fast for twelve hours, drink celery juice at sunrise, and avoid every food group except whatever the influencer is selling supplements for. It is a scam. It has always been a scam. The science is bad, the products are overpriced, and the people pushing them have abs because they have lighting and editing, not because of the protocol they are charging you for.

The phone calls. The endless phone calls in the locker room, in the cardio section, on the floor, in the sauna. Take it outside. We do not need to hear your conversation about your fantasy football league while we are trying to get through our workout. Headphones exist. Texting exists. Stepping into the parking lot exists. The fact that you are so addicted to your own voice that you cannot put it down for forty minutes is genuinely sad and very rude.

I do not have the time, energy, or patience to explain to you why your position is incoherent. Read literally any book on the subject. Read the wiki. Read the pinned posts at the top of this forum that exist specifically to address the question you keep asking. The rest of us already did the work. We owe you nothing. Stop demanding free tutoring as if your ignorance were our responsibility.

My device is no longer supported. I am informed of this via a popup that demands I upgrade my hardware to continue receiving updates. The hardware is two years old. Two years. The device cost more than a thousand dollars. The replacement is more expensive. The replacement will be unsupported in another two years. The entire industry has decided that consumer electronics are now a subscription to which we did not knowingly agree.

I am keeping a folder. Every email. Every text. Every photo of the broken appliances and the leaking pipes and the cracked tile. Every receipt for repairs I had to pay for out of pocket because you refused to do your job. The folder is thick now. Very thick. When this lease ends, the folder is going to a tenant lawyer, and you are going to wish you had spent five minutes returning my calls.

Three hundred pages of historical detail painstakingly researched and then dumped onto the page in giant unbroken paragraphs that read like a high school term paper. The author clearly loves the period. The author clearly does not love the reader. Knowing things is not the same as making a story interesting, and the inability to distinguish between the two has produced a book that doubles as a doorstop in both function and prose density.

Your security camera is pointed directly into my bedroom window. I do not need to know why you have it. I do not need to hear the explanation. I need it moved. Today. Otherwise I am calling the police and consulting a lawyer about privacy violations. The fact that you tried to deny it before I showed you the screenshot of your own publicly-shared feed tells me everything about your respect for the people who live next to you.

The valet just dented my car. I have photos from when I arrived. I have photos from when I left. The damage is on the rear passenger side, exactly where the valet would have backed into something. The valet company says they will investigate. The investigation will take six weeks. The investigation will conclude that they cannot determine the source of the damage. The fix is on me. The lawyer letter is on its way.

The official just blew his whistle for a foul that did not happen. The replay shows nothing. The player who supposedly committed the foul is two yards away from the alleged contact. The crowd booed for a solid minute. The referee did not look up, did not acknowledge it, did not admit the mistake. Just stood there with his hand on his hip like the entire stadium was wrong. The arrogance is what kills me.
